squander

SKWON-der · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To squander is to wastefully use something.

The committee accused the previous administration of squandering an entire decade of surplus tax revenue on projects that were never finished.

Worked Example

Given a full scholarship and a rare opportunity most students would treasure, he chose to squander it by skipping nearly every class.

Carelessly wasting something valuable, money, time, or an opportunity, instead of using it wisely is exactly what it means to squander it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

waste: To waste is the plain, everyday word for using something up carelessly or to no benefit — water, food, an afternoon. To squander is heavier: it means wasting something genuinely valuable — a fortune, a scholarship, a rare chance — recklessly and usually past recovering.

dissipate: To dissipate money is to let it trickle away, a little at a time, until nothing is left; the word emphasizes the gradual scattering. To squander is broader and often more sudden — recklessly wasting money, time, or a chance, whether in one blowout or in many.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

conserve: use carefully to avoid waste

save: keep for future use rather than spend

Where it sits · how wastefully the money goes — spend → squander → throw away

spend vs. squander: Spend is a milder, neutral word next to squander: anyone spends money on ordinary needs, while to squander it means wasting it recklessly on nothing of value.

throw away vs. squander: Throw away is even harsher than squander: to squander a fortune is to waste it carelessly, but to throw it away suggests total waste, as if the money meant nothing at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — squander (origin disputed)

root — squander (origin disputed): possibly from an old dialect word meaning 'to scatter' (Middle English, origin genuinely uncertain)

Put it together

Put it together: Squander's exact origin is a genuine mystery to etymologists -- it may come from an old dialect word meaning 'to scatter.' That older, literal sense of scattering something carelessly survives today only in the figurative meaning: to squander money or time is to let it scatter away to nothing.

Use the root in a new word: squander (the older sense)

Use the root in a new word: squander (the older sense): In an old shepherd's account from the 1500s, a careless boy let the flock squander across the open hillside instead of keeping it together.
